FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application

Mohan Bheemadolu ††thanks: Code: https://github.com/mohanji/flyhash-agent-memory
Archive (DOI): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23903302 Affiliation: Independent Researcher. Email: mohan.bmdl@gmail.com    Chrisogonas O. Odhiambo Affiliation: Email: chrisogonas@gmail.com
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly’s olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism — sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition — and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash’s codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash’s, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing’s practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by- embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.

1 Introduction

Large language model agents that operate over long or repeated interactions increasingly need memory: a way to store facts, preferences, or prior context and retrieve the relevant pieces on demand (Chhikara et al., 2025). The dominant approach embeds each memory as a dense vector and retrieves by approximate nearest-neighbor search over an index such as FAISS (Johnson et al., 2021; see also the RAG survey of Zhao et al., 2024), though hybrid retrieval architectures combining dense and lexical signals are an active and growing alternative. This works well but scales in memory and compute with the size and dimensionality of the stored embeddings, motivating interest in more compact representations — in particular, hashing schemes that compress an embedding into a short binary code while preserving enough neighbor structure to remain useful for retrieval.

One such scheme, introduced by Dasgupta, Stevens, and Navlakha (2017) and directly inspired by neurobiology, computes a locality-sensitive hash the way the fruit fly’s olfactory circuit is believed to encode odors: roughly 50 receptor-neuron activations are randomly and sparsely projected into approximately 2,000 “Kenyon cells,” of which only the top ∼\sim5% most active are allowed to “fire,” producing a sparse binary code. The original paper showed that this scheme — which we refer to as FlyHash, following subsequent literature — preserves nearest-neighbor structure better, at a matched number of output bits, than SimHash (Charikar, 2002), the standard random-hyperplane hashing baseline, on several benchmark datasets including SIFT, GloVe, and MNIST.

Despite this result and several follow-up papers extending the algorithm (surveyed in Section 2), we are not aware of any prior work applying FlyHash-style hashing specifically to LLM agent memory retrieval — a setting that is, in several respects, a natural fit: agent memories are frequently decomposed into short, numerous, semantically embedded units retrieved by similarity (Hu et al., 2026; Du, 2026; Zeng et al., 2024) — the regime this paper’s evaluation targets, though we note that recent work increasingly favors structured or hierarchical retrieval over flat similarity search for longer-horizon tasks (Cao et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026).

This paper is organized around three research questions, each answered precisely rather than in the aggregate, because — as we show below — the answers are not all the same shape:

  • •

    RQ1. Under a protocol that correctly holds FlyHash’s and SimHash’s active bit counts equal (Section 3.2), does FlyHash’s reported per-bit retrieval-quality advantage over SimHash hold for data representative of LLM agent memory, robustly across seeds and datasets? (Sections 4.1–4.2; answer: yes, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall that must be avoided to get there — Appendix A.)

  • •

    RQ2. Does that quality advantage translate into an actual resource advantage — lower memory, lower query latency — in a realistic deployment, including against the dense-vector indexing methods (HNSW) practitioners use by default today? (Sections 4.3–4.4, 4.6; answer: not by default, and not relative to HNSW at ordinary scale — hashing’s resource case is narrower than the quality result alone would suggest.)

  • •

    RQ3. Does the quality advantage hold under genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels, rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy used everywhere else in this literature (including the original FlyHash paper)? (Section 4.7; answer: yes.)

In service of these questions, the paper’s contributions are: (1) the first application, to our knowledge, of FlyHash to LLM agent memory retrieval, with a working end-to-end system (Sections 3.5, 4.5); (2) the matched-active-bit protocol itself, stated precisely enough to prevent a specific conflation we discovered by reproducing a discrepancy with a published result (Section 3.2, Appendix A); (3) statistical and cross-dataset validation beyond the original paper — 10 seeds, four datasets across two modalities, a 36-configuration hyperparameter sweep, and a paired statistical analysis (Sections 4.1–4.2); and (4) an honest, multi-angle resource and deployment analysis that does not stop at the quality result — brute-force memory/latency costs, a sparse-set comparison, a direct HNSW systems baseline, and a relevance-label upgrade (Sections 4.3–4.4, 4.6–4.7).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 situates this work relative to FlyHash’s original paper and its algorithmic follow-ups. Section 3 describes the method, evaluation protocol, datasets, and statistical procedure. Section 4 presents results. Section 5 discusses their implications. Section 6 states limitations and future work. Appendix A gives a full account of the reproducibility investigation that motivated the corrected protocol in Section 3.2.

2 Related Work

The original algorithm. Dasgupta, Stevens, and Navlakha (2017) introduced the algorithm this paper builds on, showing that a neurally-plausible circuit — sparse random projection into a much higher-dimensional space, followed by winner-take-all sparsification — functions as a locality-sensitive hash competitive with, and often superior to, dense random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash; Charikar, 2002) at a matched number of output bits. Their evaluation covered SIFT descriptors, GloVe word vectors, and MNIST images. This paper directly reuses their algorithm and their choice of evaluation datasets (GloVe and MNIST; we do not evaluate on SIFT — see Section 6), applying it to a problem domain they did not consider.

DenseFly. Sharma and Navlakha (2018) extended the base algorithm with “DenseFly,” which densifies FlyHash’s sparse output as a post-processing step to further improve similarity search accuracy. This is a genuine algorithmic improvement over plain FlyHash that we do not implement here; we discuss it as natural future work in Section 6.

BioHash. Ryali, Hopfield, Grinberg, and Krotov (2020) replaced FlyHash’s random sparse projection with a learned one, trained with a biologically-plausible local learning rule, and reported improved retrieval accuracy over the random-projection version across several datasets. Their paper also established mean Average Precision (mAP) as the standard evaluation metric for this line of work, which we adopt in Section 3.2. We note for transparency that BioHash’s learned projection is reported to outperform the plain FlyHash evaluated in this paper; our contribution is not a better hash function, but an application and validation of the simpler, random-projection version, which requires no training data or learning procedure — a practically relevant trade-off for a lightweight agent-memory component.

FlyNN. Most recently, work applying the fly olfactory circuit to federated nearest-neighbor classification (“FlyNN,” AAAI 2022) illustrates the breadth of problems this biological mechanism has been adapted to beyond pure hashing, extending it to a federated learning setting.

Existing implementations. A general-purpose FlyHash package is available on PyPI (Huang, MIT license), providing a NumPy-compatible implementation of the base algorithm for small-to-medium input dimensionalities. Its existence confirms that an implementation of the algorithm itself is not a novel contribution; our implementation exists to support the specific experiments in this paper rather than to serve as a general-purpose library.

Graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search. A different line of work achieves fast approximate retrieval not by compressing each vector into a short code, but by building a navigable graph over the full-precision (or lightly quantized) vectors and searching it via greedy graph traversal. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs; Malkov and Yashunin, 2016/2020) is the dominant practical method in this family and underlies most production vector-search systems in use today (e.g., FAISS’s IndexHNSW, and the default indexes in several vector databases including Milvus, Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector; Idrees et al., 2026). HNSW and hashing schemes like FlyHash and SimHash target different points in the retrieval design space: HNSW optimizes for sublinear query time and high recall at the cost of storing richer per-item structure (full or near-full vectors plus graph edges), while FlyHash and SimHash optimize for extreme per-record compactness — a short binary code compared via cheap Hamming distance — at the cost of the brute-force, linear-scan comparison this paper evaluates throughout. Our main results (Sections 4.1–4.4) isolate hashing-function quality by comparing FlyHash against SimHash at matched bit budgets, rather than against HNSW, since the two are different design points (compact-code quality versus indexed graph search); we separately report a direct, explicitly-labeled systems comparison against HNSW in Section 4 for readers asking the practical “which would I actually deploy” question.

LLM memory architectures and retrieval-augmented generation. A large and rapidly growing body of work designs memory systems for LLM agents directly, distinct from the hashing-algorithm literature surveyed above: production-oriented long-term memory frameworks (Chhikara et al., 2025), structural memory representations spanning chunks, triples, and summaries (Zeng et al., 2024), and recent surveys of agent memory mechanisms and evaluation (Du, 2026). This literature’s central recent finding — that flat, independent similarity retrieval over text snippets can suffer from redundancy and relational blindness at longer horizons, motivating structured or hierarchical retrieval instead (Hu et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026) — is complementary to this paper’s contribution: we evaluate hashing methods within the flat similarity-based retrieval regime that remains a widely used baseline (e.g., Mem0-style systems), rather than proposing or evaluating a structured memory architecture; combining FlyHash-style hashing with structured retrieval is natural future work (Section 6).

Vector quantization and alternative hashing families. A separate line of work compresses dense vectors via quantization rather than binary hashing. Product Quantization (Jégou, Douze, & Schmid, 2010) and its optimized variants (Ge et al., 2013) achieve higher retrieval accuracy than binary hashing at comparable memory budgets by preserving continuous distance estimates via asymmetric lookup tables rather than collapsing to Hamming codes; recent methods such as RaBitQ extend this advantage to extreme, 1-bit-per-dimension compression (Gao & Long, 2024). We do not evaluate against this family here, since our focus is a head-to-head comparison between two hashing paradigms under a matched-bit protocol, but it represents a stronger baseline than either hash method at most operating points — consistent with the HNSW result in Section 4.6. Within the hashing family itself, more sophisticated locality-sensitive schemes such as Cross-Polytope LSH achieve a better asymptotic query exponent than random-hyperplane hashing (Laarhoven, 2020), but this advantage only materializes at large scale and high ambient dimension; at the moderate dataset sizes evaluated here (Table 1), hyperplane-based SimHash remains competitive or superior in wall-clock performance due to lower per-hash computational overhead (Cai, 2016; Laarhoven, 2020), motivating our choice of standard SimHash, rather than Cross-Polytope LSH, as the baseline.

Sparse lexical retrieval. A different line of “sparse retrieval” work — BM25, and learned sparse lexical models such as SPLADE (Formal, Lassance, Piwowarski, & Clinchant, 2024) — operates directly on text via sparse term-weight vectors over a vocabulary, which is a distinct notion of sparsity from the sparse binary codes FlyHash derives from dense embeddings via winner-take-all competition. These lexical methods are a complementary, not competing, approach, well-suited to exact keyword matching rather than semantic similarity over learned embeddings, and are outside this paper’s scope of embedding-based hashing methods.

This paper’s position. None of the above apply FlyHash-style hashing to LLM agent memory retrieval, and none report the depth of statistical validation (multi-seed variance, multi-dataset, multi-modality, hyperparameter ablation) presented in Section 4. The gap this paper fills is at the intersection of a new, currently relevant application and a level of empirical rigor — including a documented and corrected methodological pitfall — that the base algorithm’s literature does not yet provide.

3 Method

3.1 FlyHash and SimHash

Both hashing schemes take a dense input vector x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and produce a binary output code.

SimHash (Charikar, 2002) draws a dense random matrix W∈ℝk×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d} with entries sampled i.i.d. from a standard normal distribution, and outputs

hsim​(x)=sign⁡(W​x)∈{0,1}k.h_{\text{sim}}(x)=\operatorname{sign}(Wx)\in\{0,1\}^{k}.

Every one of the kk output bits is thresholded independently; the code is dense in the sense that each bit is set to 1 with probability approximately 1/21/2.

FlyHash (Dasgupta et al., 2017) instead draws a sparse random projection matrix P∈ℝm×dP\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}, where each row (each “Kenyon cell”) is connected to only a random subset of ⌈s⋅d⌉\lceil s\cdot d\rceil input dimensions (ss is the sparsity, fixed at 0.10 throughout this paper, following the fly’s own connectivity, where each Kenyon cell integrates inputs from roughly 5–12% of input channels; Caron, Ruta, Abbott, & Axel, 2013), with weights drawn uniformly from {−1,+1}\{-1,+1\} on those connections and zero elsewhere. The projection P​xPx is then passed through a kk-winners-take-all operation: only the kk largest of the mm projected values are set to 1, all others to 0:

hfly​(x)=WTAk⁡(P​x)∈{0,1}m,∥hfly​(x)∥0=k.h_{\text{fly}}(x)=\operatorname{WTA}_{k}(Px)\in\{0,1\}^{m},\qquad\lVert h_{\text{fly}}(x)\rVert_{0}=k.

We refer to mm as the pool size (the total number of Kenyon cells, fixed at 2,000 in our experiments unless otherwise stated) and kk as the bit budget (the number of winning, active bits). This notational distinction — kk versus mm — is deliberately explicit, because conflating the two is the source of the reproducibility discrepancy described in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.

3.2 Evaluation protocol

Metric. Following BioHash (Ryali et al., 2020), we evaluate retrieval quality with mean Average Precision at RR (mAP@RR). For a query qq, let the relevant set be its RR true nearest neighbors under exact Euclidean distance on the original (unhashed) embeddings. Average Precision for qq is

AP​(q)=1R​∑ℓ=1RPrecision​(ℓ)⋅Rel​(ℓ),\text{AP}(q)=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{\ell=1}^{R}\text{Precision}(\ell)\cdot\text{Rel}(\ell),

where Rel​(ℓ)=1\text{Rel}(\ell)=1 if the item ranked ℓ\ell-th by Hamming distance under the hash code is in the relevant set, and Precision​(ℓ)\text{Precision}(\ell) is the fraction of relevant items among the top ℓ\ell ranked results. mAP@RR is the mean of AP​(q)\text{AP}(q) over all queries. Unlike plain recall@kk, mAP@RR rewards ranking true neighbors earlier, not merely including them somewhere in the top RR.

Matched-active-bit (quality-per-active-bit) protocol. The central methodological point of this paper concerns what it means to compare FlyHash and SimHash “at the same number of bits.” There are at least three distinct, non-interchangeable notions of parity one could hold fixed:

  1. 1.

    Equal active/output bits — the number of bits that are actually compared by Hamming distance per query (kk for both methods). This is the notion we use throughout Sections 4.1–4.2, and we call it the matched-active-bit protocol to avoid the vaguer, overloaded term “fair comparison.”

  2. 2.

    Equal physical storage — the number of bytes each method’s code occupies at rest, which depends on representation (dense vs. packed vs. sparse-index), not just kk (Sections 4.3–4.4).

  3. 3.

    Equal query-time/resource budget — the number of bytes moved or compared per query, which can differ from storage when a method’s on-disk and in-memory representations differ (Sections 4.3–4.4, 4.6).

Conflating these is the specific pitfall this paper is built around. Concretely, under the matched-active-bit protocol, for each bit budget kk we evaluate FlyHash with pool size mm fixed at a large value (2,000, unless stated otherwise) and the winner-take-all fraction set to k/mk/m, and we evaluate SimHash with exactly kk output bits — so both methods produce the same number of active bits, isolating the quality of the hash function from either method’s absolute output size. This is not the naive way to run the comparison: a naive implementation might instead fix FlyHash’s total output width (i.e., set mm to whatever “bits” value is being swept) and hold the winner-take-all percentage fixed (e.g., 5%, matching the fly’s own biology) — in which case FlyHash’s effective number of active bits at a given nominal “bits” value is only a small fraction of that value, while SimHash is given the full nominal count as genuinely active bits. This conflation of kk (notion 1) with mm silently and substantially disadvantages FlyHash, and is distinct from the storage/resource conflations addressed later (notions 2 and 3, Sections 4.3–4.4). We discovered the first pitfall by reproducing a discrepancy with a published result; the full diagnostic process, including hypotheses we initially pursued and later ruled out, is given in Appendix A.

3.3 Datasets

We evaluate on four independent real datasets spanning two modalities, summarized in Table 1.

All embeddings are L2-normalized prior to hashing where applicable (GloVe, MiniLM). MNIST and digits pixel intensities are scaled to [0,1][0,1].

Data availability. All four datasets are public and loaded programmatically, and none of them is redistributed in this paper’s code release: GloVe via gensim’s model downloader (https://nlp.stanford.edu/projects/glove/); MiniLM sentence embeddings via the sentence-transformers library, which downloads the pretrained checkpoint from https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2; scikit-learn’s bundled digits dataset via sklearn.datasets.load_digits(); and MNIST via OpenML (https://www.openml.org/d/554), fetched with sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml(). Exact loading code is in the repository linked on the title page. The labeled agent-memory benchmark of Section 4.7 (6,000 memories, 150 queries, relevance labels) is released as JSONL files in the same repository (datasets/agent_memory_v1/), together with an offline demo, tests, and a REPRODUCING.md guide mapping each table to a command. The release is archived on Zenodo (release v1.0; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23903302, which resolves to the latest version).

3.4 Statistical protocol

Both FlyHash’s sparse projection matrix and SimHash’s dense hyperplane matrix are randomly initialized, so a single evaluation reflects one particular random draw, not the expected behavior of the method. For our main results (Section 4.1) and hyperparameter ablation (Section 4.2), we repeat every evaluation across NN independent random seeds (10 for the main results, 3 for the larger hyperparameter sweep, given its greater number of configurations), varying only the projection matrices’ initialization across seeds while holding the dataset and the sampled set of queries fixed. This isolates projection-matrix randomness as the source of measured variance, rather than conflating it with variance from query sampling. We report the mean and standard deviation of mAP@RR across seeds, and, as a simple and intentionally conservative robustness check, whether the gap between FlyHash’s and SimHash’s mean mAP exceeds twice their combined standard deviation (Δ>2​σfly2+σsim2\Delta>2\sqrt{\sigma_{\text{fly}}^{2}+\sigma_{\text{sim}}^{2}}). We present this as a sanity check against attributing an observed gap to projection-matrix noise, not as a substitute for a formal statistical significance test.

Because FlyHash and SimHash are evaluated on the same 10 seeds (same sampled queries, same train/query split, differing only in which method’s projection matrix that seed initializes), the two methods’ mAP values at a given bit budget are naturally paired, not independent samples — each seed contributes one paired difference di=mAPfly,i−mAPsim,id_{i}=\text{mAP}_{\text{fly},i}-\text{mAP}_{\text{sim},i}. For our primary GloVe result (the first block of Table 2, and Table 3 below) we additionally report a paired analysis: the mean paired difference with both a tt-interval and a bootstrap (10,000 resamples) 95% confidence interval, the paired effect size (Cohen’s dzd_{z}), and two nonparametric tests that do not assume normality — the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and a sign-flip permutation test (10,000 permutations). This is a strictly stronger statement than the “robust” heuristic above, which compares marginal variances and discards the pairing.

3.5 Agent memory integration

To validate the practical use case motivating this work, we implement a minimal LLM agent memory system: a plain text remember(text) / recall(query, k) interface wraps a sentence-transformer embedding model and a FlyHash-backed store, so that an agent interacts only with text, not embeddings or hash codes directly. We wire this into a live tool-use loop with a general-purpose LLM exposing two tools — save_memory, called when the model judges the user has shared a fact worth remembering, and recall_memory, called when answering a question that may depend on a previously shared fact. In a representative interaction, a user states two facts in one turn (“My favorite language is Python and I’m allergic to peanuts”), asks an unrelated question in the next turn, and then asks “What should I avoid eating?” in a third turn; the agent correctly answers “peanuts” by calling recall_memory, retrieving the relevant fact via FlyHash-based Hamming-distance ranking over stored memory embeddings from several turns earlier. This demonstrates the full pipeline functioning end-to-end, independent of the benchmark-style evaluation in Section 4.

4 Results

4.1 Main result: corrected comparison across four datasets

Table 2 reports mAP@RR (mean ±\pm standard deviation over 10 random seeds) for FlyHash and SimHash at five bit budgets, on each of the four datasets described in Section 3, under the corrected protocol of Section 3.2. “Robust” indicates whether the gap between the two methods’ means exceeds twice their combined standard deviation (Section 3.4).

tt-interval and bootstrap CIs agree closely at every bit budget, and Cohen’s dzd_{z} is an order of magnitude past the conventional “large” threshold of 0.8 throughout. The Wilcoxon and permutation pp-values sit at 1/210≈0.001951/2^{10}\approx 0.00195, the smallest value either test can report with n=10n=10 paired seeds — FlyHash wins on all 10 seeds at every budget, so this is the resolution floor of the test, not a computational artifact. This paired analysis, not the “gap >> 2×\timescombined std” heuristic alone, is what we consider the primary evidence of a robust effect; the heuristic is retained in Table 2 as a quick, consistent summary across all four datasets.

FlyHash outperforms SimHash at every bit budget, on every dataset, with every gap classified robust — 20 independent (dataset, bit-budget) comparisons, zero exceptions. A consistent secondary pattern is also visible across all four datasets: the relative advantage (mAPfly/mAPsim\text{mAP}_{\text{fly}}/\text{mAP}_{\text{sim}}) is largest at the smallest bit budget and shrinks as kk grows — for example, on GloVe, FlyHash is 4.2×4.2\times SimHash at k=16k=16 but only 1.5×1.5\times at k=256k=256. Figure 1 plots this ratio against bit budget for all four datasets at once, making the shared pattern visible across modalities. We return to the significance of this pattern in Section 5.

4.2 Hyperparameter ablation

FlyHash has two hyperparameters left fixed throughout Section 4.1: sparsity ss (fraction of input dimensions each Kenyon cell samples from; 0.10 by default, following the fly’s own connectivity) and pool size mm (2,000 by default). To check whether the Section 4.1 result depends on these specific choices, we sweep s∈{0.05,0.10,0.20}s\in\{0.05,0.10,0.20\} and m∈{500,1000,2000,4000}m\in\{500,1000,2000,4000\} — 12 combinations — at three representative bit budgets (k∈{16,64,256}k\in\{16,64,256\}), on GloVe, with 3 seeds per configuration (fewer than Section 4.1’s 10, given the larger number of configurations swept here).

All 36 configurations exceed the SimHash baseline at their respective bit budget — no combination of sparsity and pool size reverses the result. Two secondary patterns are visible: sparsity somewhat above the fly’s own biological ratio (0.20 vs. ≈\approx0.10–0.12) performs marginally better at larger bit budgets, and increasing pool size beyond roughly 8×8\times the bit budget yields diminishing or slightly negative returns. Neither pattern threatens the main result; both are minor tuning observations. Figure 2 renders Table 4 as heatmaps, which makes both secondary patterns easier to see at a glance than the raw numbers.

4.3 Memory and query latency: quality gains do not imply resource gains

The results above measure retrieval quality only. We separately measure memory footprint and query latency on GloVe (5,000 records), comparing FlyHash and SimHash at matched kk against an exact (unhashed) Euclidean nearest-neighbor baseline, using brute-force comparison for all three (no approximate index on either side).

FlyHash’s code is not itself kk bits wide — it is mm bits wide (2,000 in our default configuration), of which exactly kk are active. Our default dense representation stores and compares this full mm-bit array regardless of kk, which makes FlyHash’s packed size a near-constant ∼\sim250 bytes/record independent of kk — larger than SimHash’s genuinely kk-bit code at every budget tested except k≳250k\gtrsim 250 — and its brute-force query time a near-constant ∼\sim13 ms/query, 10–70×\times slower than SimHash at the same kk. This is a real structural property of the dense representation, not a bug: mAP depends only on which kk bits are active, so it is entirely unaffected, but memory and speed under this representation clearly are.

4.4 A sparse-set comparison: partial recovery

Because every FlyHash code has exactly kk active bits, the Hamming distance between two such codes reduces to 2​k−2​|A∩B|2k-2|A\cap B|, where AA and BB are their sets of active indices. Ranking by Hamming distance is therefore identical to ranking by descending intersection size, which we compute as a sparse-sparse matrix product over only the active indices, rather than a dense operation over the full mm-wide array.

The sparse comparison is 10–22×\times faster than the dense comparison and, unlike the dense version, its latency correctly scales with kk rather than remaining flat. It does not, however, close the gap to SimHash entirely: SimHash’s small dense k×kk\times k matrix multiplication remains 2–5×\times faster at every budget tested, and explicit index-list storage, while now also correctly scaling with kk, remains ∼\sim16×\times larger than SimHash’s bit-packed code, since storing an explicit position costs a full integer where bit-packing costs a single bit. We report this as a genuine, partial improvement — not a solved problem — and discuss the remaining gap in Section 6.

4.5 Agent memory demonstration

The end-to-end system described in Section 3.5 functions correctly: in the representative interaction described there, the agent retrieves a fact shared several turns earlier via FlyHash-based Hamming ranking over MiniLM sentence embeddings, without that fact appearing anywhere in the immediate conversational context. This confirms the pipeline is functional for its intended use case, independent of the benchmark numbers in Sections 4.1–4.4.

As one measured data point for the full pipeline’s latency (embedding included, not just the isolated hash comparison of Sections 4.3–4.4), we timed a single representative query against the 6,000-record corpus of Section 4.7, averaged over 30 repeats on consumer hardware, using the sparse-set comparison method of Section 4.4 for the hash-ranking step (the same method behind Table 6’s speed numbers, consistent with the rest of the paper rather than an unrelated, unoptimized implementation):

With the hash-ranking step measured consistently with Table 6, sentence embedding — not FlyHash’s hash comparison — is the dominant cost of the full pipeline, by roughly 2:1. This is a useful finding in its own right: it means that, at this corpus size, FlyHash’s own contribution to end-to-end latency is modest relative to the (hash-independent) embedding step, and that further latency optimization in a real deployment would pay off more from the embedding stage than the hash comparison. Embedding time is identical regardless of which hash is used downstream, so this number has no bearing on the FlyHash-vs-SimHash comparisons elsewhere in the paper — it exists only to put a real figure on the full pipeline’s latency rather than leaving it unmeasured. We still report it as a single data point on one machine, not a benchmark: no seed averaging and no variation in corpus size or hardware. A proper system-level benchmark remains future work (Section 6).

4.6 Practical systems comparison: FlyHash/SimHash vs. a graph-based ANN index

Sections 4.1–4.4 hold the active-bit budget kk fixed and compare FlyHash against SimHash — both compact hash codes compared by Hamming distance. This answers “which hash is better at a given bit budget,” but not “would I actually use either of these instead of a standard production ANN index.” We report that second, separate question here using FAISS’s IndexHNSWFlat (M=32M=32, efConstruction=200=200) over full-precision GloVe vectors (5,000 records, 50 queries, mAP@100), explicitly as a systems comparison rather than a matched-bit one: HNSW has no “bits” parameter comparable to kk, so its quality/speed/memory trade-off is governed by efSearch instead, and the two tables below should be read within themselves, not row-matched against each other.

At this scale, HNSW dominates both hash methods on quality and latency simultaneously — mAP above 0.98 and sub-0.1ms queries, at only ∼1.6×\sim 1.6\times the raw exact-storage memory cost (671.5 vs. 400 bytes/record) — while FlyHash and SimHash’s only genuine advantage is extreme compactness well below exact storage (as little as 2–32 bytes/record). The honest conclusion is that a practitioner with no unusual memory constraint and a dataset at this scale should use HNSW, not a hash code; FlyHash/SimHash’s relevance is specifically to the regime HNSW does not target — severe, explicit storage budgets (e.g., many independent memory stores on resource-constrained agents) — and we revise our framing in Section 5 accordingly rather than letting Sections 4.1–4.4 imply a general retrieval recommendation.

4.7 A realistic, labeled agent-memory benchmark

Every result above uses nearest-neighbor-by-embedding as a stand-in for “relevance” — two items are treated as relevant to each other if an unhashed embedding considers them close, which is circular with respect to the embedding itself and does not test anything about whether hashing preserves true query-to-memory relevance. We address this with a separate benchmark using constructed relevance labels that do not derive from any embedding distance.

Established agent-memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) evaluate end-to-end conversational QA accuracy over multi-session dialogue, which conflates retrieval quality with the downstream LLM’s reasoning over retrieved context (Wu et al., 2024, explicitly separate indexing, retrieval, and reading for this reason). Our evaluation instead requires ground-truth relevance labels for the retrieval step in isolation — the quantity FlyHash and SimHash actually compete on — which these QA-style benchmarks do not provide directly. We therefore construct a dataset with explicit, non-circular relevance labels anchored to named personas below, in the same spirit as recent calls for benchmark designs that disentangle retrieval correctness from answer correctness (Wu et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2026).

Construction. We generate 150 synthetic named personas, each with 10 independent facts (favorite color, allergy, job title, hometown, and six others), each fact expressed via 3–4 paraphrase templates that name the persona directly (e.g., “Jordan’s favorite color is teal.” / “If you ask Jordan, teal is their favorite color.”), giving 6,000 memory sentences total. Each query is a differently-worded question that also names a target persona (e.g., “Which color does Jordan like best?”), and its ground-truth relevant set is exactly that persona’s own paraphrases for that fact (3–4 sentences out of 6,000) — a label fixed by construction, not by embedding similarity. Naming every fact and question to a specific persona is what makes the corpus both genuinely confusable (thousands of near-identical same-template statements about other people crowd every query) and answerable from text content alone (the one token that correctly disambiguates the right answer — the name — is actually present in the query), which an earlier, unnamed version of this design was not: without a persona name tying question to answer, no text-similarity method, hashed or not, can identify whose stated value is correct among many textually identical same-template statements, and we do not report numbers from that earlier, ill-posed version.

Embedding. We embed both memories and queries with TF-IDF followed by truncated SVD (256 components), fit on the memory corpus — an offline, network-free stand-in for a real sentence-transformer embedding, consistent with this project’s practice elsewhere (Section 6).

FlyHash beats SimHash robustly at every budget on this genuinely-labeled task, with absolute mAP values well above chance (random ranking over 6,000 items with ∼\sim4 relevant would score far below 0.1) but, expectedly, lower than Table 2’s nearest-neighbor-pseudo-label mAP — this is a harder, more realistic task by construction, and the two numbers are not meant to be compared directly. This result is, to our knowledge, the first time FlyHash’s advantage over SimHash has been shown against actual, non-circular relevance labels for an agent-memory-shaped task rather than an embedding-similarity proxy.

5 Discussion

Why is the advantage largest at low bit budgets? FlyHash’s sparse expansion into a much higher-dimensional space before selecting winners appears to preserve more of the input’s neighborhood structure per output bit than SimHash’s direct dense projection, particularly when very few bits are available to encode that structure. As the bit budget grows, both methods have enough capacity to represent more of the relevant structure, and the relative gap narrows — though FlyHash’s absolute advantage never disappears across any budget we tested (Table 2). This pattern is practically significant: real deployments of compact hashing are motivated precisely by wanting few bits per record (that is the entire point of hashing over storing full embeddings), so the regime where FlyHash’s advantage is largest is also the regime a real system would actually operate in.

A quality advantage is not automatically a resource advantage. Section 4.3 is, to our knowledge, an underappreciated point in this line of work: a hash function can preserve neighbor structure strictly better than a baseline while, in a naive implementation, being simultaneously worse on memory and speed — because “better structure per bit” and “cheap to store and compare” are different properties that do not automatically follow from each other. Section 4.4 shows that a principled fix targeting the comparison’s sparsity recovers much, but not all, of one axis (speed) while leaving the other (memory) only partially improved. We think this distinction — quality-per-bit versus deployed resource cost — is worth making explicit in any evaluation of a hashing scheme derived from a sparse-coding argument, not only in this paper.

Practical implication for agent memory. An agent adopting FlyHash today obtains a genuine, robustly validated retrieval-quality improvement per bit over SimHash, particularly in the low-bit-budget regime most relevant to a resource-constrained memory system, and (Section 4.7) that advantage survives contact with genuine, non-circular relevance labels, not just an embedding-similarity proxy. It should not, on the basis of this paper, expect a memory or latency improvement over a well-implemented SimHash baseline without further engineering (Section 6), nor should it expect either hash method to beat a standard production ANN index such as HNSW at ordinary scale (Section 4.6) — HNSW wins on quality and latency simultaneously there, at a modest memory premium over exact storage. Which of these properties matters most depends on the deployment: a system already committed to compact hash codes, bottlenecked on retrieval accuracy at a fixed, small bit budget, benefits from FlyHash as a drop-in SimHash replacement; a system with no unusual storage constraint should likely use HNSW instead of either hash; and a system bottlenecked specifically on raw per-record storage at a scale where even HNSW’s overhead is unaffordable is the narrow regime where FlyHash/SimHash-style hashing is the right tool at all.

6 Limitations and Future Work

  • •

    Memory and speed do not fully match the quality advantage, even after a targeted attempt to close the gap. Section 4.4’s sparse-set comparison recovers most of the speed disadvantage but leaves a meaningful memory disadvantage; a genuinely sublinear index (e.g., banded or multi-probe LSH, or an inverted index verified sublinear at scale — an earlier inverted-index attempt in our own implementation was found not to be sublinear at the scales we tested) remains unbuilt. A more compact encoding of the active-index list (delta-coding of sorted indices, variable-length or entropy coding, or reducing pool size at some cost to quality) is a concrete, identified next step we did not pursue here.

  • •

    Our HNSW comparison (Section 4.6) is a single-scale, single-configuration snapshot. We report one dataset (GloVe, 5,000 records) and one HNSW configuration (M=32M=32, efConstruction=200=200, three efSearch values); HNSW’s relative advantage over hashing shrinks as per-record storage budgets tighten and may shrink or reverse at very different corpus scales, which we have not swept. A combined approach (e.g., FlyHash codes as a cheap pre-filter ahead of an HNSW-indexed re-ranking stage, in the spirit of how FAISS combines quantization with HNSW) is a natural direction we have not explored.

  • •

    SIFT1M, part of the original paper’s evaluation, is not included. We judged that four independent datasets across two modalities already provide strong evidence the result is not dataset-specific, and that a fifth, necessarily subsampled dataset (SIFT1M’s full 1M-vector scale is impractical to evaluate exhaustively at our compute budget) would add breadth rather than materially new evidence. We report this as a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight.

  • •

    We do not implement DenseFly’s densification or BioHash’s learned projection, both of which are reported improvements over the plain, random-projection FlyHash evaluated here (Section 2). Combining either with the agent-memory application is natural future work.

  • •

    We compare two hashing paradigms (sparse random-projection vs. dense random-hyperplane) but do not benchmark against vector quantization methods (e.g., Product Quantization, RaBitQ), which the literature indicates generally outperform hashing in accuracy-per-bit (Jégou et al., 2011; Gao & Long, 2024; Section 2); a comparison against quantization is natural future work alongside the HNSW baseline already included.

  • •

    The real-text (MiniLM) evaluation uses a small, 100-sentence corpus, chosen to avoid duplicate-embedding artifacts (see Appendix A) rather than to represent realistic agent-memory scale. A larger, more diverse real-text corpus would strengthen this specific result.

  • •

    We report only a single data point for the full end-to-end agent memory system’s latency (Section 4.5: 20.5 ms/query on one machine, one query, 30 repeats), not a proper benchmark — no seed averaging and no sweep over corpus size or hardware. A dedicated, multi-seed system-level benchmark is future work.

  • •

    The realistic, labeled agent-memory benchmark (Section 4.7) uses templated synthetic text, not naturally-occurring language, and a TF-IDF+SVD embedding as a stand-in for a real sentence-transformer. Real sentence diversity is considerably messier than any fixed template set, and real deployments would more plausibly scope memory retrieval by session or user ID than rely on a name mentioned in free text. A rerun with real human-written memory logs and a real sentence-transformer embedding (on a machine with internet access, the same gap already noted for MiniLM/MNIST elsewhere in this paper) would strengthen this specific result.

7 Conclusion

Our three research questions have three different shapes of answer, and we state the claim no wider than that. FlyHash beats SimHash at matched active-bit counts, robustly, on every dataset and seed we tested, including under genuine agent-memory relevance labels rather than an embedding-similarity proxy (RQ1, RQ3) — this is a real, well-supported result, and one previously undocumented comparison pitfall (kk-vs-mm conflation) had to be corrected to see it. But the practical deployment question (RQ2) does not resolve as cleanly: FlyHash’s quality advantage over SimHash does not translate into a memory or latency advantage under a naive comparison, a sparse-set comparison closes most but not all of that gap, and a standard production index (HNSW) outperforms both hash methods on every axis at ordinary scale, leaving genuinely extreme storage constraints as hashing’s specific niche rather than a general deployment recommendation. We think this — a validated hash-quality result, a corrected methodological pitfall, and a resource picture that narrows rather than flatters the headline claim — is a more useful contribution to reproducible progress here than a report that stopped at the first, more flattering result.

Appendix A Reproducibility Investigation

While reproducing the original paper’s reported result on GloVe word vectors, we initially found FlyHash losing to SimHash on every dataset we tried — synthetic clustered embeddings, TF-IDF text vectors, real sentence embeddings, and real GloVe vectors — directly contradicting the published finding on GloVe. We treated this discrepancy as a signal that our comparison, not the algorithm, was most likely at fault, and pursued it systematically rather than accepting or explaining away the contradiction.

Hypotheses ruled out. We first tested whether L2-normalizing inputs before hashing affected the result; it did not, meaningfully. We then tested whether using the algorithm’s exact original weight definition (true binary {0,1}\{0,1\} projection weights, rather than the signed {−1,+1}\{-1,+1\} weights we had implemented) affected the result; it did not, and we quantify this claim across all five main bit budgets below rather than resting it on the single seed we checked at the time. We then tested whether our evaluation metric — recall@kk by overlap, rather than mAP@RR — was responsible; switching to mAP@RR produced the same qualitative picture. Each ruled-out hypothesis narrowed the search space without resolving the discrepancy.

Quantifying the weight-mode claim. The “it did not, meaningfully” judgment above was originally made on a single seed. Re-run across all 10 seeds and all five main bit budgets (GloVe), with SimHash included as a reference:

Both weight modes beat SimHash by a wide margin at every budget tested. The signed-vs-binary difference is not zero and grows with kk (0.004 at k=16k=16 to 0.058 at k=256k=256), so the honest claim is not “no difference” but “small relative to the FlyHash-vs-SimHash effect at every budget we tested, with a modest upward trend at higher kk” — the main results in Section 4.1 use the signed variant throughout, and this table bounds how much of that result could plausibly be an artifact of that choice.

The actual cause. We resolved the discrepancy by comparing our implementation’s parameterization directly against a third-party reference implementation of the original algorithm (github.com/dataplayer12/Fly-LSH). This revealed that our comparison held FlyHash’s total hash dimensionality equal to SimHash’s bit count while separately fixing FlyHash’s winner-take-all percentage — silently making FlyHash’s effective number of active bits, at any given nominal “bits” value, a small fraction of what SimHash was being given as its full, genuinely active bit count. This is precisely the kk-versus-mm conflation described in Section 3.2. Correcting the protocol to hold kk (not mm) equal between the two methods, with mm fixed independently at a large value, immediately reproduced the original paper’s reported pattern: FlyHash winning decisively on GloVe at every bit budget, and — as it turned out — on every other dataset we subsequently tested as well (Section 4.1).

A hypothesis retracted. Prior to finding this cause, we had observed that FlyHash appeared to outperform SimHash specifically on data with correlated, non-negative features (e.g., TF-IDF text vectors) but not on isotropic synthetic data, and had proposed that FlyHash specifically benefits from such data properties. Once the actual comparison bug was corrected, this pattern disappeared: FlyHash outperformed SimHash on the corrected synthetic isotropic data just as decisively as on text data. We state plainly that our earlier hypothesis was incorrect — it was constructed to explain an artifact of a flawed comparison, not a genuine property of either the data or the algorithm — and we retract it here rather than omit it from this account.

We document this investigation in this level of detail because the underlying pitfall — conflating a hash’s effective bit count with its nominal parameter dimensionality — seems easy to make and is, to our knowledge, not explicitly warned against elsewhere in this literature. We hope stating it precisely, alongside the specific hypotheses that seemed plausible but were not the actual cause, helps others attempting a similar comparison avoid the same error.
